name: Kolam
basis: why: drawn in rice flour at the door each morning round a lattice of dots; how: loops and diamonds per square, flour with grainy edges on a floor
note: The dot-grid rule is geometric; the flour line is the process.

lumenary.blurb: Rice-flour floor drawing from South India. Lines loop around a grid of dots; where your picture is dark the loops thicken into diamonds and petals.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with clear light and dark areas

why: In Tamil Nadu and the south of India, women draw a kolam at the door each morning in rice flour, so that ants and birds are fed as they pass. The most common kind starts with a lattice of dots, called pulli, and a line that loops round them. The patterns are made by simple rules, and the same dots can make many different drawings. Here each square of four dots chooses its figure from the tone of your picture.
how: Place dots on a square lattice with the chosen spacing.

For each square of four dots, draw loops (quarter circles of radius s/2 about each corner, turning inward, so four neighbouring squares draw a full circle round the shared dot), a diamond joining the midpoints of the four sides, both, or nothing.
Choose by the tone t (less the density slider): empty if t ≥ 0.78, loops only if 0.62 ≤ t < 0.78, diamond only if 0.4 ≤ t < 0.62, and both if t < 0.4, so dark places turn into diamonds and petals.
Fold the point where the picture is read for mirror symmetry, and in four-fold symmetry fold the top and bottom as well.
Draw the flour as a canvas of its own with grainy edges and a soft glow, laid over a floor texture.
history: Kolam is drawn daily, and in the month of Margazhi (December to January) streets fill with large, elaborate ones. Related floor drawings include rangoli in much of India, muggu in Andhra Pradesh and alpana in Bengal. Mathematicians and computer scientists have studied kolams since the 1970s, as pictures made by simple rules, and Gift Siromoney and colleagues in Chennai were among the first to analyse them with array grammars.
uses: Daily floor art and festival decoration
Computer science research on picture languages
terms: A floor drawing made of rice flour or paste, drawn at the threshold.
The dots that form the lattice of a kolam.
A set of rules for generating pictures on a grid.
paragraphs: In Tamil Nadu and the south of India, women draw a kolam at the door each morning in rice flour, so that ants and birds are fed as they pass. The most common kind starts with a lattice of dots, called pulli, and a line that loops round them. Mathematicians and computer scientists have studied kolams since the 1970s, as pictures made by simple rules. The program places dots on a square lattice with the chosen spacing, and for each square of four dots it decides which of two figures to draw from the tone of your picture.

The first figure is the loop round the dots. A quarter circle of radius s/2 is drawn about each corner of the square, turning inward, so that four neighbouring squares draw a full circle round the dot they share, and the circles of neighbouring dots touch at the middle of the edge between them. The second figure is the diamond joining the midpoints of the four sides. For the tone t (less the density slider), a square is empty if t ≥ 0.78. It has only the loops if 0.62 ≤ t < 0.78, only the diamond if 0.4 ≤ t < 0.62, and both if t < 0.4, which is why dark places turn into diamonds and petals. Symmetry is made by folding the point where the picture is read, so that the left and right (and with four-fold symmetry the top and bottom) read the same tones. The flour is a canvas of its own, with grainy edges and a soft glow, laid over a floor texture.
